summary.text: The cosmic microwave background is a faint glow of microwave radiation that fills all of space and comes from no star or galaxy.
It dates from when the young universe cooled enough for atoms to form, which let light travel freely for the first time.
It is very smooth, yet maps show tiny temperature ripples whose pattern tells us about the early universe.

facts.label: Discovered
facts.value: By accident in 1964, by Penzias and Wilson

facts.label: Temperature
facts.value: About 2.7 kelvin, with a thermal black body spectrum

facts.label: Smoothness
facts.value: Uniform to roughly one part in 25,000

items.prompt: An astronomer points a very sensitive radio telescope at a patch of sky between stars and galaxies. What would she most likely pick up?

options.label: A faint, nearly uniform glow tied to no object
Total silence, because the space is empty
A bright signal from one hidden distant star
Scattered bursts from clumps of nearby galaxies

items.explain: Optical telescopes see dark gaps, but radio telescopes detect a faint, nearly uniform glow that belongs to no star, galaxy or other object.

items.prompt: Why could light finally travel freely through the young universe?

options.label: The plasma heated up and blew the fog away
Stars switched on and cleared the dense plasma
Charged particles joined into neutral atoms that stopped scattering light
Expansion stretched light until it could not be scattered

items.explain: As the universe cooled, protons and electrons combined into neutral atoms. Unlike the plasma, these could not scatter thermal radiation, so the universe became transparent.

items.prompt: Photons released long ago are now far weaker than when they were set free. What explains their lower energy?

options.label: They lost energy by hitting stars on the way
They were stretched by the expansion of the universe
They were absorbed by neutral hydrogen atoms
They weakened because they are very old

items.explain: The photons have grown less energetic because of the cosmological redshift that comes with the expansion of the universe.

items.prompt: A friend says the night sky should be dark because stars are the only source of light. How does the glow of this background compare to all starlight ever emitted?

options.label: It is far too weak to compare
It is about the same amount
It is a small fraction of it
Its energy density is greater

items.explain: The energy density of the background exceeds that of all the photons emitted by all the stars in the history of the universe.

items.prompt: Cosmologists see the background as very smooth, yet spend years mapping it. Why do the tiny differences matter?

options.label: Their pattern carries clues about the early universe
They show exactly where each future star will form
They are measuring errors that scientists must remove
They mark the positions of the nearby planets

items.explain: The ripples form a pattern whose peaks hold important information about the early universe, including its overall curvature and the density of matter.

items.prompt: Researchers want to compare the glow's brightness across many wavelengths. What makes one number, its temperature, enough?

options.label: The glow is made of a single wavelength
A black body's temperature fixes its intensity at every wavelength
Wavelengths do not matter for microwave light
Temperature and brightness are unrelated here

items.explain: The blackbody temperature uniquely characterizes the intensity of the radiation at all wavelengths, so a brightness at any wavelength converts to a temperature.

paragraphs.heading: A glow behind everything
paragraphs.text: Look between the stars and galaxies with an ordinary optical telescope and the background is nearly black. Point a radio telescope that is sensitive enough at the same spot, though, and a faint glow shows up that is almost the same everywhere and belongs to no star, galaxy or other object. This glow is the cosmic microwave background, or CMB, and it fills all of space in the observable universe. It is brightest in the microwave part of the electromagnetic spectrum.

paragraphs.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs.text: The CMB is the main piece of observed evidence for the Big Bang theory of how the universe began. American radio astronomers Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson came across it by accident in 1964, capping work that had started in the 1940s. Long before that, in 1931, Georges Lemaître guessed that traces of the early universe might be seen as radiation, but he thought they would be cosmic rays. In 1934 Tolman showed that an expanding universe would cool blackbody radiation while keeping its thermal spectrum.

paragraphs.heading: Where the light came from
paragraphs.text: In Big Bang models, the earliest universe was filled with an opaque fog: a dense, hot plasma of sub-atomic particles. As space expanded, that plasma cooled until protons and electrons joined into neutral atoms, mostly hydrogen. Atoms, unlike the plasma, could not scatter thermal radiation by a process called Thomson scattering, so the universe turned transparent. This moment, the recombination epoch, set the photons free to cross space. Ever since, the redshift that comes with cosmic expansion has drained energy from them. The surface of last scattering is the shell of space at just the right distance for light released at that moment to be reaching us now.

paragraphs.heading: Cold and very even
paragraphs.text: The CMB arrives from every direction as uniform black body thermal energy. It is measured in kelvin (K), the SI unit of temperature, and its spectrum matches a black body at 2.72548±0.00057 K. It is strikingly smooth, quite unlike the near point-like look of stars and galaxies. Once a dipole is removed, caused by the Doppler shift of the Sun moving at 369.82 ± 0.11 km/s toward the constellation Crater, the sky is even to roughly one part in 25,000.

paragraphs.heading: Tiny ripples with big meaning
paragraphs.text: Sensitive maps still pick up small but important temperature differences, and ground and space experiments such as COBE, WMAP and Planck have measured them. These uneven spots, called anisotropies, form a pattern of tiny ripples shaped by how matter and light interacted up to decoupling. Broken down by angular scale, they give a power spectrum with a series of peaks and valleys. The first peak fixes how curved the universe is overall; the second and third show, in turn, the density of normal matter and of dark matter.

paragraphs.heading: A sky full of old photons
paragraphs.text: The CMB holds the great majority of the universe's photons, outnumbering all others 400 to 1. Its photons are a billion (10⁹) times more numerous per unit volume than matter, with about 411 in every cubic centimetre. Their energy today is far greater than that of all the light every star has ever given off. Had the expansion of the universe not cooled this radiation, the night sky would blaze as brightly as the Sun.
